props.html:
The remarks are done, the lights come down a little, and the band that played through dinner is suddenly loud enough to dance to. Getting a party to that moment is mostly a budget problem, because ideas lists never come with numbers, so every option you bring back opens a second research project into what it costs, and the party gets planned at the speed of the slowest quote.

This list runs the other way. Each idea below comes with the build it actually needs, which moves a number far more than the choice of act does. For the budget itself: a cover or jazz band for a corporate event runs $2,500 to $8,000 in the Colorado market, and Denver bands run $2,500 to $8,000, with a trio at the bottom of that and a full band with horns at the top. How prices like those are built is set out in what live music costs for a corporate event, and the sourced market table is on the pricing page. Where the party goes is its own decision, and the sixteen Denver venues are covered one by one in the Denver venue guide.

Our artists have played for Amazon, NBCUniversal, Charles Schwab, Kroger, the Denver Art Museum, Sheraton, Hyatt, the Washington Nationals, Casa Bonita and Monarch Casino, and the formats below are the ones nights like those take.

props.text: Christmas party entertainment that leaves space for the conversation

props.html:
Ask a group of planners what to bring to a Christmas party and you get magicians, mentalists, tarot readers and a casino night, and then somebody says the whole category is played out. What they’re reaching for underneath the list is narrower than it looks. They want something that gives the evening a center and still leaves space for the conversation, because the argument they make for the magician is that guests get a reason to stop and talk to each other.

A trio does that for the whole evening. Guitar, upright bass and drums played with brushes sit at a level two colleagues from different floors can introduce themselves across. It asks nothing of anybody: guests drift toward the musicians, stand there a minute, and carry the conversation back to wherever they were standing before. The evening ends up with a middle to it that nobody had to organize.

That’s also the answer to the fear of forced fun. An act that plays isn’t an activity your people have to agree to join, and a night with music in it never has the flat stretch where the catering has been cleared and nothing has replaced it.

The DJ is the most common single booking of the corporate season, and the simplest to approve: one line and one load-in, with the whole night covered. An open-format DJ reads the crowd from the first drink to the last song.

This is the idea to pitch when the budget line is the point. Across the Colorado market a DJ carrying a night with production lighting runs $2,500 to $6,000, under what a band of any size costs for the same hours, and it still holds a dance floor.

This is for the party that’s really a dinner: a seated evening, a toast or two, and conversation as the main event. The jazz duo plays standards on upright bass and guitar at a level people talk across without leaning in. Three hours is the usual length.

If the group outgrows the duo, the trio adds drums played with brushes for larger floors. A jazz trio or acoustic duo for a dinner runs $500 to $3,000 in the Colorado market, which is the range this idea sits in.

Not every office party leaves the office, and the format that fits a catering spread on the main floor at the end of a workday is a small one. A single hour of the acoustic duo is a real booking: voice and guitar playing covers people know at a volume they can talk across. A solo guitarist is smaller again, and fits an office floor without moving the desks.

A quartet covers a four-hour evening, playing dinner at conversation volume and getting loud on cue when the program ends and the night turns. This is the booking for a party where the dancing is the point, and four musicians is what a ballroom floor actually needs. The horns and the second vocalist are what take a booking into show-band money, at $7,500 to $17,000.

The flagship version is Tejas Singh: a duo through arrival and dinner that grows to a quartet when the dancing starts, same voice, same songs, one contract. Guests hear one band getting bigger.

This is the full-evening configuration for a crowd that will outlast the band: a quartet for three hours, then a DJ carrying the late end through the same sound system on the same contract. Because the setup is already paid for, adding that hour costs far less than a second booking would. It comes to a five-hour evening with two different kinds of music in it, on one contract and one invoice.

The band plays the 80s and 90s hits on its own, sung out front, and hands the microphone to anyone in the crowd who wants a song, with the words on a screen and a host on the floor. The band fills the set on its own, and it’s ready the moment somebody gets brave. You can book it as its own night or as the loud chapter of a longer one. The live band karaoke page has the songbook and the builds.

Some parties want one thing guests photograph, and a format none of them have seen at an office party before. Dirty Flamenco is that booking: real palos played by a working flamenco trio, with a dancer configuration when the night wants a floor show. It’s the entertainment as the centerpiece of the party.

props.text: Holiday party entertainment ideas for large groups

props.html:
Most of the seven scale, but not all of them scale the same way, and the number that decides it is the headcount. A dinner for forty and a ballroom of two hundred and fifty are two different acoustic problems, and the format that fixes the second one is bigger than the format that fixes the first.

Under about eighty guests, the duo carries the whole evening on its own. Two musicians in a corner, and nothing about the setup announces itself and the music reaches every table.

Between eighty and about a hundred and fifty, the trio is the size to book. Drums played with brushes are what let the sound stay conversational while covering twice the floor. This is the band most large Denver office parties actually need, and it’s smaller than the one they usually ask about first.

Above a hundred and fifty, the quartet is the size a floor that has to fill actually needs. That’s four musicians, playing dinner at conversation volume and getting loud on cue when the program ends. A hotel ballroom of two hundred with a short program in front of the dancing is what this build exists for.

Two things go wrong at scale regardless of size. The first is that a large group breaks into a dozen separate conversations within minutes of arriving, so an entertainment idea that only reaches the people queuing for it reaches a small share of the guest list. The second is the venue’s own audio. A house system specified for speeches won’t carry a band across a full ballroom, which is why sound support that’s the right size for the venue is part of the booking here.

props.text: What the calendar does to the number

props.html:
Denver holiday parties get decided between August and October, and the calendar does most of the moving. There are 21 party dates across November and December, Thursdays through Saturdays, and a peak December date costs more than a standard one everywhere in the Colorado market: a Denver holiday weekend carries 20 to 30 percent. New Year’s Eve is a case of its own, and it books earlier than anything else on the calendar.

These prices come from published 2026 market guides, read September 2026. We quote each date one-by-one.

The season’s dates, with the peak ones marked, are laid out on the holiday party page, and whether yours is free is a two-line email: the date and the venue.

props.text: The Christmas party that happens in January

props.html:
A real share of Denver companies now hold the Christmas party after the new year, and the planners who moved it say the same two things about why. December belongs to everybody else, and a January party is a party your people can actually attend without three competing invitations on the same evening.

Everything on this list works in January and one thing works better. The evening stops competing with the season it was named after, so a format that wants attention gets it: the set piece, the live-band karaoke chapter, the quartet that takes a floor. The music is also the part of the night that carries a January date without explanation, because standards and covers aren’t seasonal repertoire and never needed a tree behind them.

If the date is already in January, the useful thing to know is that the whole conversation moves outside the eight weeks every other holiday booking is fighting over. Seven ways to run that evening, themes included, are in January office party ideas.

props.title: If the venue isn't booked yet either
props.html: The entertainment decision and the venue decision usually run in parallel, and the venue’s fine print moves the music budget more than most planners expect: in-house catering mandates, start-time rules and load-in windows all live in the venue contract. The Denver venue guide reads sixteen of Denver’s venues the way we read a space before we play it.
